window_text.1: Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
window_text.2: He was the one who rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after Amaziah rested with his ancestors.

blind.question: Who is replaced as king?

assessments.reason: The text says they “made him king in place of his father Amaziah,” directly indicating that Amaziah was replaced as king.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly states that Uzziah was made king in place of his father Amaziah, identifying Amaziah as the one replaced.

reader.quote: made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
reader.contrast: Amaziah, the king being replaced, versus Uzziah, the person installed as king.
reader.reason: The window explicitly says Uzziah was made king in place of Amaziah. The wording clearly asks for the displaced king, and answering requires distinguishing the predecessor from his successor.

editor.quote: made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
editor.contrast: Amaziah is the king whose place is taken; Uzziah is the new king who takes his place.
editor.reason: The phrase “in place of” clearly identifies Amaziah as the predecessor being replaced and Uzziah as his replacement, resolving the plausible role reversal.

items.question: Who did Zechariah teach to fear God?

window_text.3: Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years. His mother’s name was Jekoliah; she was from Jerusalem.
window_text.4: He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, just as his father Amaziah had done.
window_text.5: He sought God during the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God. As long as he sought the Lord, God gave him success.

items.original_question: Whom does the instructor teach to fear the Lord?
items.original_answer: Zechariah teaches Uzziah to fear God.

edit.question: Who did Zechariah teach to fear God?
edit.reason: Names Zechariah so the reader only needs to resolve who received his instruction.

blind.question: Who did Zechariah teach to fear God?

readings.support: Uzziah | who instructed him in the fear of God

assessments.reason: Verse 5 says, “He sought God during the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God,” where “he/him” refers back to Uzziah in verses 3–4.

blind.reason: The text explicitly states that Zechariah instructed “him” (Uzziah) in the fear of God.

editor.quote: He sought God during the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God.
editor.contrast: Uzziah as the person Zechariah instructed versus Amaziah, who is mentioned only as Uzziah’s father.
editor.reason: Amaziah is a plausible distraction because he is named immediately beforehand, but he appears only in a comparison with Uzziah. Uzziah remains the subject of “He sought God,” and “him” refers back to Uzziah, so the key is uniquely supported. Resolving that reference makes this a meaningful comprehension question.

reader.quote: He sought God during the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God.
reader.contrast: Uzziah, the subject referred to by “He” and “him,” versus his father Amaziah.
reader.reason: The passage continues describing Uzziah, so “him” refers to Uzziah. Identifying the student requires resolving the pronoun rather than confusing him with the previously mentioned Amaziah.

items.question: Where does Uzziah rebuild towns?
items.answer: Near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.

window_text.6: He went to war against the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod. He then rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.
window_text.7: God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabs who lived in Gur Baal and against the Meunites.
window_text.8: The Ammonites brought tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread as far as the border of Egypt, because he had become very powerful.

items.original_answer: Near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.

blind.question: Where does Uzziah rebuild towns?

readings.answer: Near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.
readings.support: near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines

assessments.reason: The answer exactly matches the passage: "He then rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines."

blind.reason: The reading directly matches the verse stating he rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.

reader.quote: He then rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.
reader.contrast: The places where Uzziah rebuilt towns versus the cities whose walls he broke down.
reader.reason: The passage directly locates the rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines. Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod are instead named as cities whose walls he destroyed.

editor.quote: He then rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.
editor.contrast: The rebuilt towns were near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines, whereas Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod were places whose walls he broke down.
editor.reason: The window directly and uniquely identifies where he rebuilt towns. The question tests whether the reader distinguishes the rebuilding locations from the cities attacked in the preceding sentence.

items.question: What does Uzziah fortify after building in Jerusalem?

window_text.9: Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, at the Valley Gate and at the angle of the wall, and he fortified them.
window_text.10: He also built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, because he had much livestock in the foothills and in the plain. He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.

items.original_question: What does Uzziah fortify after building in Jerusalem?

blind.question: What does Uzziah fortify after building in Jerusalem?

readings.support: built towers in Jerusalem | he fortified them

assessments.reason: The passage says Uzziah “built towers in Jerusalem… and he fortified them,” so “them” clearly refers to the towers he built.

blind.reason: “He fortified them” directly refers to the towers Uzziah built in Jerusalem.

reader.quote: Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, at the Valley Gate and at the angle of the wall, and he fortified them.
reader.contrast: Whether “them” refers to the towers or to the gates.
reader.reason: The towers are what Uzziah built, while the gates identify their locations, so “them” refers to the towers. Resolving that pronoun reference distinguishes the key from the plausible gate misreading.

editor.quote: Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, at the Valley Gate and at the angle of the wall, and he fortified them.
editor.contrast: Whether “them” refers to the towers Uzziah built or to the nearby gates.
editor.reason: The gates are a plausible distraction because they are nearby plural nouns, but “at” identifies them as locations. The direct object of “built” is “towers,” so “fortified them” refers to the towers.

items.question: Under whose command are the 307,500 trained men?

window_text.11: Uzziah had a well-trained army, ready to go out by divisions according to their numbers as mustered by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer under the direction of Hananiah, one of the royal officials.
window_text.12: The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600.
window_text.13: Under their command was an army of 307,500 men trained for war, a powerful force to support the king against his enemies.
window_text.14: Uzziah provided shields, spears, helmets, coats of armor, bows and slingstones for the entire army.
window_text.15: In Jerusalem he made devices invented for use on the towers and on the corner defenses so that soldiers could shoot arrows and hurl large stones from the walls. His fame spread far and wide, for he was greatly helped until he became powerful.

items.original_question: Under whose command are the 307,500 trained men?

assessments.reason: Verse 12 identifies 2,600 family leaders, and verse 13 says “Under their command was an army of 307,500,” so “the 2,600 family leaders over the fighting men” matches the key.

blind.reason: “Under their command” in verse 13 clearly refers back to the 2,600 family leaders in verse 12.

editor.quote:
The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600.
13  Under their command was an army of 307,500 men trained for war
editor.contrast: The 2,600 family leaders as the men’s direct commanders versus Uzziah as the king whom the army supported.
editor.reason: Uzziah is a plausible alternative because he is the king associated with the army, but “their” refers to the immediately preceding plural group, the 2,600 family leaders. Resolving that reference is necessary to identify who commanded the 307,500 men.

reader.quote:
The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600.

reader.contrast: The 307,500 men were under the 2,600 family leaders, not directly under Uzziah.
reader.reason: The reader must resolve “their” to the family leaders named immediately before it. The passage explicitly states both their number and their command over the army.

items.question: Why is Uzziah eager to leave?
items.answer: Because the Lord has afflicted him.
items.competitor: Because the priests hurry him out.

window_text.19: Uzziah, who had a censer in his hand ready to burn incense, became angry. While he was raging at the priests in their presence before the incense altar in the Lord’s temple, leprosy broke out on his forehead.
window_text.20: When Azariah the chief priest and all the other priests looked at him, they saw that he had leprosy on his forehead, so they hurried him out. Indeed, he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.

items.original_question: Why is Uzziah eager to leave?
items.original_answer: Because the Lord has afflicted him.

readings.answer: Because the Lord had afflicted him.
readings.support: because the Lord had afflicted him

assessments.reason: Verse 20 explicitly says he was eager to leave because the Lord had afflicted him, matching the key’s wording.

blind.reason: The passage directly states he was eager to leave because the Lord had afflicted him.

reader.quote: he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.
reader.contrast: The reader must distinguish why Uzziah himself wanted to leave from the priests’ separate action of hurrying him out.
reader.reason: The passage directly identifies the Lord’s afflicting Uzziah with leprosy as the cause of his eagerness to leave. The priests’ response is related but is not presented as the reason for his own eagerness.

editor.quote: he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.
editor.contrast: Whether Uzziah wants to leave because the priests are forcing him out or because the Lord has afflicted him.
editor.reason: The explicit because-clause identifies the Lord’s affliction as the reason for Uzziah’s own eagerness, while distinguishing it from the priests’ action of hurrying him out.

items.question: Why is Uzziah buried near his family, not with them?
items.answer: Because people said he was leprous.
items.competitor: Because the cemetery belongs to the kings.

window_text.21: King Uzziah had leprosy until the day he died. He lived in a separate house—leprous, and banned from the temple of the Lord. Jotham his son had charge of the palace and governed the people of the land.
window_text.22: The other events of Uzziah’s reign, from beginning to end, are recorded by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
window_text.23: Uzziah rested with his ancestors and was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.” And Jotham his son succeeded him as king.

items.original_question: Why is Uzziah buried near his family, not with them?
items.original_answer: Because people said he was leprous.

blind.question: Why is Uzziah buried near his family, not with them?

readings.answer: Because people said he had leprosy.

assessments.reason: Verse 23 explicitly gives the reason: he was buried near them "for people said, 'He had leprosy,'" which matches the key's wording.

blind.reason: The passage states he was buried near the kings because people said he had leprosy.

editor.quote: was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.”
editor.contrast: Uzziah’s leprosy as the reason for burial near his ancestors versus the royal cemetery as merely the burial location.
editor.reason: The causal word “for” links his burial near, rather than with, his ancestors to people saying that he had leprosy. The cemetery’s ownership identifies the place but does not give the reason for the separation.

reader.quote: was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.”
